title: Acute mesenteric ischaemia: recognition, imaging and revascularisation

guidelineVersions: ESVS Clinical Practice Guidelines on the Management of Diseases of the Mesenteric and Renal Arteries and Veins (2025)

related.why: Acute limb ischaemia: the same embolic source and urgency

brief.role: Core surgical trainee in general surgery
brief.scenario: Mr Brian Galloway, 72, has had sudden severe central abdominal pain for three hours. He has vomited and opened his bowels once. He has atrial fibrillation and stopped his apixaban two weeks ago after nosebleeds. Pulse 112 irregular, BP 104/68. His abdomen is soft and only mildly tender. Venous lactate is 4.5 mmol/L.
brief.task: Discuss the likely diagnosis and his management with the examiner.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Severe pain, soft abdomen, AF: mesenteric ischaemia until CT angiography says otherwise.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Being reassured by a soft abdomen, or waiting for the lactate to decide.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "I'm worried about acute mesenteric ischaemia from an SMA embolus."

grid.label: Recognition
grid.fail: Diagnoses gastroenteritis or constipation because the abdomen is soft.
grid.pass: Suspects acute mesenteric ischaemia: pain out of proportion to signs, gut emptying and AF off anticoagulation.
grid.high: Names the embolic triad and says peritonism is a late sign of infarction, not a requirement for diagnosis.

grid.label: Resuscitation and escalation
grid.fail: Sends him for imaging without resuscitation or a senior informed.
grid.pass: ABCDE, oxygen, IV access, fluids, bloods with gas and group and save, catheter; escalates to the registrar and consultant.
grid.high: Starts IV antibiotics and involves vascular surgery, interventional radiology and critical care early.

grid.label: Interpreting lactate
grid.fail: Says a normal lactate would exclude ischaemia, or waits for it to rise.
grid.pass: A single lactate or D-dimer cannot confirm or exclude the diagnosis.
grid.high: A high lactate reflects systemic hypoperfusion and risk of death, not bowel ischaemia specifically.

grid.label: Imaging
grid.fail: Requests plain films or ultrasound, or delays CT because of renal function.
grid.pass: Urgent CT angiography in arterial and venous phases, stating suspected mesenteric ischaemia on the request.
grid.high: Proceeds regardless of renal function; looks for SMA occlusion, poor bowel wall enhancement, pneumatosis and portal venous gas.

grid.label: Causes
grid.pass: Arterial embolism, arterial thrombosis, mesenteric venous thrombosis and non-occlusive mesenteric ischaemia.
grid.high: Thrombosis follows prior post-prandial pain and weight loss; non-occlusive ischaemia follows low-flow states and vasopressors.

grid.label: Definitive treatment
grid.fail: Plans bowel resection alone, or conservative treatment of an arterial occlusion.
grid.pass: Urgent revascularisation (endovascular first line, or open embolectomy) in a centre with 24/7 vascular services; laparotomy to assess and resect non-viable bowel if suspected.
grid.high: Revascularises before resecting; resects without anastomosis and plans a second look.

grid.label: Prognosis and decisions
grid.fail: Offers false reassurance, or does not discuss ceilings of care.
grid.pass: Explains that about half of patients die in hospital and involves him and his family early.
grid.high: Recognises a palliative approach may be right for extensive necrosis in a frail patient, decided with him and seniors.

pass.speaker: candidate

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Why aren't you reassured by his soft abdomen?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: This is the embolic triad: severe pain with few signs, gut emptying, and an embolic source. Peritonism means the bowel is already infarcting.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: IV antibiotics now, and early calls to vascular surgery, interventional radiology and critical care.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: So what does the lactate tell you?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: It reflects systemic hypoperfusion and risk of death. It isn't a specific marker of bowel ischaemia.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'd still do the CT angiogram; the guideline says regardless of renal function. I'd look for SMA occlusion, poor bowel wall enhancement, pneumatosis and portal venous gas.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: How would a thrombotic occlusion differ?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Often a history of post-prandial pain and weight loss. Non-occlusive ischaemia follows low-flow states such as cardiogenic shock or vasopressors.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Revascularisation, so viable bowel declares itself. Then resect without anastomosis and plan a second look.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: If CT showed extensive necrosis in a frail man, a palliative approach may be kinder. That's a decision with him, his family and my consultant.

failures.move: Being reassured by a soft abdomen.
failures.consequence: Early reversible ischaemia progresses to infarction while he waits.

failures.move: Using lactate to rule mesenteric ischaemia in or out.
failures.consequence: A normal early lactate delays CT angiography.

failures.move: Avoiding contrast because of renal impairment.
failures.consequence: The diagnosis is delayed; the guideline advises CT angiography regardless of renal function.
The occlusion persists and more bowel dies.

recovery.when: The examiner stresses the soft abdomen
recovery.line: Pain out of proportion to the signs is exactly what worries me here.
It tells me how sick he is, not whether the bowel is ischaemic; CT angiography decides.

knowledge.fact: Embolic SMA triad: severe pain with minimal signs, gut emptying, and an embolic source such as AF.
A single lactate or D-dimer should not be used to confirm or exclude the diagnosis.
Urgent CT angiography in arterial and venous phases, regardless of renal function.
Treat in a centre with 24/7 open and endovascular expertise; revascularise before resection; second look.
Give antibiotics. Venous thrombosis: anticoagulation first line.
In-hospital mortality is about half (49% in the prospective AMESI study).

recall.think: Bowel infarction and death; the soft abdomen is early, not reassuring.
recall.say: "Suspected acute mesenteric ischaemia: I need CT angiography now."
do: CT angiography, arterial and venous phases
recall.trap: A soft abdomen or a normal lactate.
recall.finish: Revascularisation, resection of non-viable bowel, second look.

media.task: Identify the SMA occlusion and signs of bowel ischaemia
media.description: Axial and sagittal CT angiogram showing an abrupt filling defect in the superior mesenteric artery a few centimetres beyond its origin, with thin-walled, poorly enhancing small bowel loops

partner.opening: Here are his observations and lactate. What do you think is going on?

reveals.finding: Occlusive embolus in the SMA beyond the first jejunal branches; small bowel enhancing normally; no pneumatosis.
No previous abdominal pain on eating, no weight loss.

push.question: His lactate is 4.5. Does that confirm the diagnosis?
push.expect: No: a single lactate cannot confirm or exclude it.

push.question: Which imaging, and would his renal function change that?
push.expect: CT angiography, arterial and venous phases, regardless of renal function.

push.question: CT shows an SMA embolus. What happens next?
push.expect: Urgent revascularisation, endovascular first line or open, in a centre with 24/7 vascular services; laparotomy if non-viable bowel is suspected; revascularise first.

push.question: What will you tell his family?
push.expect: About half die in hospital; early, honest discussion and ceilings of care.

curveballs.prompt: CT shows superior mesenteric vein thrombosis instead.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Heparin anticoagulation is first line; laparotomy only for peritonitis or infarcted bowel.

curveballs.prompt: He is on noradrenaline in ICU after cardiac surgery and CT shows patent vessels.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Non-occlusive mesenteric ischaemia: correct the low-flow state; consider intra-arterial vasodilator (papaverine) via interventional radiology; laparotomy if peritonitis.

curveballs.prompt: At laparotomy the whole small bowel and right colon are black.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Likely unsurvivable: close, discuss with the consultant and family, palliative care.
